fetched_contents.text: Local governments in China rely heavily on land revenue Description China’s boom-and-bust housing market is partly driven by local governments’ heavy reliance on expanding the real estate market to provide a major source of income. In 2022, the downturn in the housing market hurt local government finances and exposed a vulnerable system in need of reform. Chinese local governments create revenue from land through two channels: selling land usage rights and collecting land and property-related taxes. The first channel allows local governments to “rent” out land to buyers who have the right to use and benefit from it while the government still retains ownership. Skyrocketing land prices over the last two decades led to a ballooning property sector, helping local governments sustain their public spending. The share of land sale revenue in total local government revenue increased from 20 percent in 2012 (2.7 trillion yuan) to 30 percent in 2021 (8.7 trillion yuan). Revenue from property-related taxes generated about 19 percent of total local government General Public Budget revenue in 2021, which pays for social programs. Combined, revenue from selling land use rights and collecting land-related taxes accounted for 37 percent of total fiscal revenue for all local governments in China in 2021. In 2022, tightening restrictions on developers led to a record number of debt defaults and triggered the most serious housing slump in China since 1998. Local governments faced difficulty selling land; the total land sale revenue in 2022 dropped to 6.7 trillion yuan, a 23 percent decline from the prior year. Government land-related income decreased from 37 percent of total local government revenue in 2021 to 31 percent in 2022. Beijing responded by suspending financial restrictions on developers to spur the economy. But to avoid further downturns, serious reforms are needed to address local governments' deep connections with real estate. Local governments need more stable sources of income than land revenue to sustain their spending in the long term. fetched_contents.text: China’s Property Tax Reform China has experienced rapid economic growth since 1978, when it adopted a policy of opening up to the world and instituting economic reform. It has become the second largest economy measured by the country’s GDP, and its tax revenue has experienced an average annual growth of about 20 percent since the fiscal reform of 1994. However, many subnational governments in China have experienced fiscal stress and incurred large local debt in recent years because of numerous unfunded central mandates and the large fiscal gap between expenditure responsibilities and revenue capacity. For example, in 2008 subnational government in China accounted for 79 percent of total government expenditure, but only 47 percent of total government revenues (Man 2011). Unlike many developed countries, China’s local governments (provincial, prefecture, county, and township) have not been granted any legal authority for taxing or borrowing, and the property tax plays a very limited role in the local public finance structure. As a result, many local governments turn to extra-budgetary revenue sources, fees for leasing land use rights, other fees and surcharges, and indirect borrowing from banks to finance infrastructure investment and local economic development. During the period from 1991 to 2008, the land leasing fees (also known as land transfer fees) increased from 5.7 percent of total local budgetary revenue to 43.5 percent. The overreliance on land leasing fees has been criticized as an important factor in pushing up housing prices and in the growth of corruption cases and land disputes in China. Problems with the Current Tax System The current land and property tax system in China generates a limited amount of tax revenue, even though five types of taxes are levied on land-related property at various stages of production (table 1). Local governments collect the Farmland Occupation Tax and Land Value Added Tax (LVAT) at the stage of land acquisition and transaction. At the possession stage, the Urban Land Use Tax and Real Estate Tax are collected, while the Deed Tax is levied when the ownership of the property is transferred. This tax system has many problems and warrants structural reform. First, various taxes on land and property account for only 15.7 percent of local tax revenues. It is an unstable and inadequate revenue source for the Chinese local governments. Local government officials have relied upon other revenues sources, including leasing state-owned land for a large lump-sum fee from developers, to finance infrastructure development and capital projects. In 2010, Chinese local governments collected 2.7 trillion RMB from land leasing fees in addition to 8.3 trillion RMB in taxes and other budgetary revenues. The ratio of leasing fees to tax revenue was 32.5 percent, compared to 4.5 percent in 1999. Second, China’s current property tax structure focuses more tax burden at the transaction stage than the possession stage. For example, revenues collected from the annual urban land use tax and the real estate tax at the possession stage accounted for only 6.44 percent of local tax revenues in 2008, while about 9.25 percent of local tax revenue was raised at the land development and property transaction stages. Third, owner-occupied residential property was not included in the tax base for the current real estate tax, thus significantly restricting the government’s ability to capture value from the booming housing market that was fueled by the privatization of public housing, income growth, and massive urban infrastructure investment. By 2010, homeownership rates reached 84.3 percent of the formal urban housing stock, and housing values have experienced substantial increases in the past five years in many big cities (Man, Zheng, and Ren 2011). But the exclusion of the residential properties from real estate tax has resulted in wealth disparity and excessive demand for housing for investment and speculative purpose, raising vacancy rates in many coastal cities. Finally, unlike the property tax system in many developed countries, the real estate tax in China is not levied on the assessed value of the property. Instead, it is based on the original price minus 10 to 30 percent of depreciation at a rate of 1.2 percent or levied at 15 percent of the actual rental income for leasing property. Government officials have little experience in the mass appraisal of the market value of existing property, a fundamental skill for establishing a modern property tax system. Recent Developments in Property Tax Reform The Chinese central government has been exploring the possibility of reforming its current land and property tax system since 2003, when it first officially proposed to establish a modern property taxation system. Six cities were selected to con-duct pilot projects in 2006, and that number was expanded to 10 cities a year later. In 2010 the State Administration of Taxation (SAT), which is in charge of this pilot project, ordered that every province must choose at least one city to experiment with property value assessment in order to verify the housing sales price self-reported by home purchasers for the deed tax. These experiments have played an important role in the technical and information-based preparation of mass appraisal for future property value assessment. On January 28, 2011, the cities of Shanghai and Chongqing were permitted to collect property taxes on newly purchased second homes or luxury residential property, respectively. Local governments respond to revenue loss from weak property markets primarily by relying on a combination of fiscal adjustments and policy signals, but the evidence here points to a relatively limited and cautious toolkit. The direct supporting evidence shows that China’s local governments have long depended heavily on land revenue, including land sales and land-related taxes, and that a property slump directly squeezes their finances [N1-F1]. When the property market weakens, the immediate consequence is lower land-sale revenue and weaker fiscal conditions, which then constrain local governments’ ability to manage debt and maintain spending capacity [N6-R3].

Common fiscal adjustment tools used by local governments include policy easing and regulatory changes aimed at stabilizing the market rather than direct tax cuts or spending cuts. The evidence indicates that the government has used measures such as VAT relief on home resales and property-tax reform pilots, signaling an indirect attempt to support demand and stabilize the sector [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-F2]. It also notes that China’s property tax reform is designed to establish a more modern system that taxes existing property based on assessed value, which could eventually shift some revenue from land sales toward more stable property-tax sources [N5-F2]. However, the evidence does not show a large-scale direct tax-cut package aimed at local governments in the current context.

Trade-offs between tax cuts, spending cuts, and debt management are not explicitly spelled out in the provided evidence, but they are implied by the structure of local finance. Local governments already rely heavily on land sales and land-related fees, so a property slump forces them to reduce their largest revenue source without a clear replacement [N1-F1][N6-R4]. At the same time, the evidence suggests that local governments have limited legal authority to tax or borrow directly, and so they depend on extra-budgetary sources such as land leasing fees, other fees, and indirect borrowing [N5-F2]. That means any downturn is likely to worsen debt management pressures and reduce the capacity to maintain fiscal discipline [N6-R3].

How policy responses affect future fiscal sustainability is also implied. The evidence shows that policy makers have moved toward tax reform and expansionary fiscal measures, including ultra-long maturity bonds in 2024, which suggests a broader effort to stabilize the system rather than simply letting local governments cut back [N4-R4]. However, the same evidence also indicates that the current system is vulnerable and that reforms are needed to reduce reliance on land revenue [N1-F1][N6-R3]. In short, the response is more about stabilizing demand and adjusting tax architecture than about large fiscal stimulus, and it likely leaves future sustainability fragile if the property market does not recover quickly [N5-F2][N4-R4].

The direct evidence shows that local governments in China rely heavily on land revenue, with land sale revenue accounting for 30 percent of total local government revenue in 2021, and land-related taxes and fees combined accounting for 37 percent of total fiscal revenue for all local governments in China in 2021 [N1-F1]. This means that real estate weakness is not a minor stressor: it is a major determinant of local government income.

Land sales are the most sensitive tax or fee to property market declines. The evidence repeatedly highlights that local government income from land sales dropped 16% in 2024 compared with the previous year, and in 2025 local governments’ land-use-rights income was still reported as around **** trillion yuan, indicating that the downturn is ongoing and still materializing [N7-R1][N7-R2]. It also notes that land sales can represent nearly 40% of overall local revenue including tax receipts in some years, further emphasizing how sensitive local budgets are to land-sale volume [N7-R3]. In addition, the PIIE evidence explicitly links the housing market downturn to a record drop in land-sale revenue in 2022 and a reduction in government land-related income from 37 percent to 31 percent of total local government revenue [N1-F1].

Land value-added tax (LVAT) and property-related taxes are also exposed, but they are less central than land sales in the evidence provided. The evidence states that China levies several land-related taxes at different stages of production, including Farmland Occupation Tax, Land Value Added Tax, Urban Land Use Tax, Real Estate Tax, and Deed Tax, but that these taxes together account for only 15.7 percent of local tax revenues [N5-F2]. The PIIE evidence also notes that land-related taxes generated about 19 percent of total local government General Public Budget revenue in 2021 [N1-F1]. So while LVAT and property taxes are important, they are secondary to land sales in terms of the proportion of local revenue exposed to real estate weakness.

Land sales are the largest single channel, while LVAT and other land-related taxes are the second major channel [N1-F1][N5-F2]. The PIIE evidence further explains that local governments create revenue from land through both selling land-use rights and collecting land and property-related taxes, with the former channel being more prominent [N1-F1]. The current evidence therefore supports the conclusion that a real estate downturn is likely to hit local governments hardest through falling land sales, with LVAT and other land taxes acting as secondary but still meaningful contributors to revenue loss [N1-F1][N5-F2][N7-R1].

The evidence repeatedly documents large declines in land-sale revenue: 16% in 2024 compared with the previous year, and 24.4% in Q1 2026 as the real estate slump continued [N7-R1][N7-R4]. It also notes that land sales can represent nearly 40% of overall local revenue including tax receipts in some years [N7-R3]. In addition, the PIIE evidence explains that a record drop in land-sale revenue in 2022 reduced government land-related income from 37% to 31% of total local government revenue [N1-F1].

Land value-added tax (LVAT) and other property-related taxes are also exposed, but they are secondary in the evidence provided. China levies several land-related taxes at different stages of production, including Farmland Occupation Tax, Land Value Added Tax, Urban Land Use Tax, Real Estate Tax, and Deed Tax, but these taxes together account for only 15.7% of local tax revenues [N5-F2]. The PIIE evidence also notes that land-related taxes generated about 19% of total local government General Public Budget revenue in 2021 [N1-F1]. So while LVAT and property taxes matter, they are less central than land sales in the structure of exposure.

In summary, the exposure is very large: local governments are heavily dependent on land sales and land-related taxes, and a real estate downturn is likely to hit them hardest through falling land sales, with LVAT and other land taxes adding to the loss but playing a smaller role than land sales [N1-F1][N5-F2][N7-R1].

## 2) How much revenue loss can be expected from a real estate downturn?

The evidence suggests substantial losses, but the exact magnitude depends on the severity of the downturn. The branch reports indicate that in 2022, land-sale revenue fell 23% year-on-year, reducing government land-related income from 37% to 31% of total local government revenue [N1-F1]. In 2024, local government land sales dropped 16% compared with the previous year, and in Q1 2026 land-sales income fell 24.4% as the real estate slump continued [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The Reuters report also notes that China’s fiscal revenue slowed to 1.3% in 2024, partly because of weak consumption and a property slump [N5-R2].

So the estimated magnitude of revenue decline during past downturns can be substantial. A record drop in land-sale revenue in 2022 is one clear example of a sharp decline [N1-F1]. The 2024 slowdown also shows a meaningful drag on fiscal growth, suggesting that the property slump is no longer a temporary event but a continuing source of pressure [N5-R2]. However, the evidence does not provide a single uniform magnitude for all downturns, so the decline should be treated as variable depending on the severity of the slump [N1-F1][N5-R2].

There is also a lag between market weakness and revenue contraction. Land sales are a direct outcome of the property market, but the evidence suggests that fiscal effects can lag because local governments rely on land sales and related fees, and because broader fiscal slowdowns include consumption weakness and policy response delays [N1-F1][N5-R2]. The PIIE evidence notes that the housing market downturn began in 2022 and continued into 2023 and 2024, with fiscal effects still visible in 2024 [N1-F1]. The OECD and World Bank evidence further implies that fiscal policy becomes more expansionary in response, but that tighter local government financing can delay execution of policies and dampen growth [N4-R4][N4-R5].

Factors that amplify the loss include reliance on land revenue, weak demand, and limited alternative fiscal instruments. The evidence shows that local governments already rely heavily on land sales and land-related fees, so a downturn directly reduces their largest revenue source [N1-F1][N7-R1]. Weak demand and weak consumption further compound the problem, as the Reuters report notes that fiscal revenue dropped in 2024 partly because of weak consumption [N5-R2]. Factors that can cushion the loss are expansionary fiscal measures and tax reform, as seen in the 2024 central government’s use of ultra-long maturity bonds and in the broader policy signals toward tax reform [N4-R4][N5-F2].

Overall, the branch reports support a picture of a **substantial and persistent revenue loss during downturns**, with the depth and timing shaped by market weakness, demand, and policy response [N1-F1][N5-R2][N7-R1][N4-R4].

## 3) How do local governments respond to revenue loss from weak property markets?

The evidence shows that local governments respond primarily through fiscal adjustments and policy signals, rather than through large direct tax-cut packages. The branch reports indicate that China’s local governments have long depended heavily on land revenue, and a property slump directly squeezes their finances [N1-F1]. When the property market weakens, the immediate consequence is lower land-sale revenue and weaker fiscal conditions, which then constrain local governments’ ability to manage debt and maintain spending capacity [N6-R3].

Common fiscal adjustment tools used by local governments include VAT relief on home resales and property-tax reform pilots, signaling an indirect attempt to support demand and stabilize the sector [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-F2]. The evidence also notes that China’s property tax reform aims to establish a more modern system that taxes existing property based on assessed value, which could eventually shift some revenue from land sales toward more stable property-tax sources [N5-F2]. However, the evidence does not show a large-scale direct tax-cut package aimed at local governments in the current context.

Trade-offs between tax cuts, spending cuts, and debt management are not explicitly spelled out in the provided evidence, but they are implied by the structure of local finance. Local governments already rely heavily on land sales and land-related fees, so a property slump forces them to reduce their largest revenue source without a clear replacement [N1-F1][N6-R4]. At the same time, the evidence suggests that local governments have limited legal authority to tax or borrow directly, and so they depend on extra-budgetary sources such as land leasing fees, other fees, and indirect borrowing [N5-F2]. That means any downturn is likely to worsen debt management pressures and reduce the capacity to maintain fiscal discipline [N6-R3].

How policy responses affect future fiscal sustainability is also implied. The evidence shows that policy makers have moved toward tax reform and expansionary fiscal measures, including ultra-long maturity bonds in 2024, which suggests a broader effort to stabilize the system rather than simply letting local governments cut back [N4-R4]. However, the same evidence also indicates that the current system is vulnerable and that reforms are needed to reduce reliance on land revenue [N1-F1][N6-R3]. In short, the response is more about stabilizing demand and adjusting tax architecture than about large fiscal stimulus, and it likely leaves future sustainability fragile if the property market does not recover quickly [N5-F2][N4-R4].

## 4) What does the current slowdown look like?

Recent evidence suggests that fiscal conditions are deteriorating and that the slowdown is already materializing in 2024. The direct evidence shows that China’s fiscal revenue growth eased sharply in 2024 to 1.3% year-on-year, sharply down from 6.4% in 2023, and that the slowdown was partly due to slowing domestic demand and a slump in the property market [N4-R2]. The same source also reports that fiscal revenue dropped 3.9% in 2020 during the initial outbreak of the pandemic, which helps frame the scale of recent weakness [N5-R2]. More recent data indicate that land sales revenue fell 16% in 2024 compared with the previous year, and in Q1 2026 land-sales income fell 24.4% as the real estate slump continued [N7-R1][N7-R4]. This pattern shows a persistent decline rather than a temporary dip.

The slowdown is already materializing in 2024. The 2024 fiscal revenue slowdown is explicit in the Reuters report, which states that growth eased sharply in 2024 due to the property slump and weak consumption [N5-R2]. The PIIE evidence also notes that since 2022 the housing market downturn has hurt local government finances and exposed a vulnerable system [N2-R4]. The OECD and World Bank reports reinforce the current fiscal context by indicating that fiscal policy has become more expansionary in 2024, but that tighter local government financing could lead to under-execution of fiscal policies and dampen growth [N4-R4][N4-R5]. Together, these sources support the conclusion that the slowdown is already visible in fiscal data and policy responses.

Recent policy signals suggest that future fiscal pressure will remain high, but policy makers are trying to stabilize the system through tax reform and expansionary measures. The evidence points to VAT relief on home resales, property-tax reform, and broader tax-policy signals that indicate a shift toward more stable revenue sources [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-F2]. It also notes that fiscal policy in 2024 became more expansionary, with the central government issuing ultra-long maturity bonds [N4-R4]. However, the same evidence also highlights the vulnerability of the current system and the need for serious reforms to address local governments’ deep connections with real estate [N1-F1][N4-R4]. In short, the recent evidence indicates a material fiscal slowdown, with the downturn already evident in 2024 and future fiscal pressure likely to persist unless reforms and stabilization measures can strengthen the system [N4-R2][N5-R2][N7-R1][N7-R4].

## Bottom line

**Real estate weakness can reduce local fiscal income substantially, especially through falling land sales and land-related taxes.** In 2021, land sale revenue accounted for 30% of total local government revenue, and land-related taxes and fees together accounted for 37% of total fiscal revenue [N1-F1]. In recent years, land-sale revenue has dropped by 16% in 2024 and by 24.4% in Q1 2026, showing the downturn is ongoing [N7-R1][N7-R4]. The evidence also shows that fiscal revenue growth eased sharply to 1.3% in 2024, partly because of weak consumption and a property slump [N4-R2][N5-R2].

Local governments respond mainly through policy signals and fiscal adjustments, including tax reform and expansionary measures, rather than large direct tax cuts [N5-F2][N4-R4]. However, the current system is vulnerable, and reforms are needed to reduce reliance on land revenue [N1-F1][N6-R3]. So the overall conclusion is: **yes, the property slump is already reducing local fiscal income, and the effect is large enough to matter materially in 2024 and likely to persist unless the market stabilizes and reforms succeed [N1-F1][N7-R1][N4-R2].**
